newsitem.title: SPAIN: Cuban-Spanish relations on brink over envoy crisis.
newsitem.headline: Cuban-Spanish relations on brink over envoy crisis.

text.p: Spain and Cuba were on the brink of a breakdown in relations on Tuesday after Havana, angered by Madrid's new hard line against Cuban leader Fidel Castro, withdrew its acceptance of an incoming Spanish ambassador.

Explaining its move in a statement in the Communist Party daily Granma, Cuba accused Spain of "flagrant interference" in recent statements and efforts to push its European Union partners into a tougher stance against Castro's Communist government.
Spain's conservative government in turn angrily warned Cuba that it had made a major blunder by withdrawing the formal acceptance granted last month to new ambassador Jose Coderch.

"It's a big mistake, in a word," Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told state radio. "It looks more like an unjustified tantrum than a serious, responsible reflection on the blockade Cuba is under."
Spain's outgoing ambassador, Eudaldo Mirapeix, was formally notified by Cuban authorities in the small hours of Tuesday that his successor would no longer be welcome.
"They got our (current) ambassador out of bed before dawn," a Spanish official told Reuters.
In formal terms, Havana withdrew its "placet" (Latin for "it pleases"), the official acceptance by a host country of the nomination of another state's ambassador.
"Between two countries that still have diplomatic relations, this is the strongest possible form of protest," said the Spanish official, who asked not to be named.
Witholding the "placet" before it was given would have been tantamount to a freeze in relations, but to give it first and then take it back was a much harsher step, the official added.

Havana's move caps weeks of growing tension with Madrid, where Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar has broken with the friendly approach towards Castro espoused by his predecessor Felipe Gonzalez during 13 years of Socialist rule.
At Aznar's behest, Spain is now urging its EU partners to take a harder line against Castro to conform with United States efforts to push for democracy in Cuba, including a ban on trade.

Envoys from the 15 EU states are due to discuss Spanish proposals in Brussels this week. Diplomats expect EU foreign ministers next month to endorse a paper urging Castro's government to move towards democracy and open a dialogue with the Roman Catholic church and other organisations.
Castro blasted Aznar, without actually naming him, in a speech on Sunday, accusing him of taking money from what he described as a mafia of Cuban exiles in Miami.

Gonzalez, who is now head of the Spanish opposition, taunted his successor last week for his get-tough approach to Cuba, saying Madrid's European partners would be only too happy to exploit any vacuum in economic ties.
The conservative government, which took office in May, responded by saying its new policy towards Castro was shared by "the entire civilised world, except Gonzalez."
